text: An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four decimal numbers separated by dots, like 192.168.1.10. Every address splits into a network portion and a host portion, and the subnet mask is what tells a device exactly where that split happens.

Writing out a full subnet mask gets tedious, so CIDR notation expresses the same thing as a slash and a number — the count of network bits. The formula for usable hosts in any subnet is 2 to the power of the host bits, minus 2, since every subnet reserves its first address as the network address and its last as the broadcast address.

Take 192.168.1.0 slash 27 as a worked example. A slash 27 leaves 5 host bits, so 2 to the 5th is 32 total addresses, minus 2 reserved equals 30 usable host addresses — from .1 through .30, with .0 as the network address and .31 as the broadcast address.

Why subnet at all instead of one giant flat network? Three reasons: it contains broadcast traffic within a smaller boundary, it isolates and secures groups of devices from each other, and it makes routing and troubleshooting dramatically easier by mapping a subnet to one physical location or logical group.
Next lesson: IPv4 versus IPv6 — why the address space you just learned is running out, and what the next generation of IP addressing actually looks like.
